skyline.text: Why Amit Varma ranks in­no­va­tion below the rule of law
How a cow town in Alabama be­came an R&D cap­i­tal
Why physics trav­els but so­cial sci­ence must be home­grown

brief.head: Patents tell all

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the state and innovation
lead.head: Hire the lab, don’t build it

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 59

play.label: Hear the case, step by step

body: Should the Indian state spend money to make in­no­va­tion hap­pen at all? Amit Varma and Ajay Shah ar­gued about that for much of the episode. On how it should go about it, if it must, they ended up agree­ing.

The oc­ca­sion was a paper by Shah with the sci­en­tist RA Mashelkar and Susan Thomas, *Rethinking innovation policy in India*. Varma, who finds most aca­demic pa­pers turgid, praised its “clear lan­guage”. {059-R01}

Shah started from free­dom.[[x1]] Left alone, he said, a so­ci­ety will in­no­vate by it­self. But knowl­edge leaks, through pub­li­ca­tions, patents, ma­chines that can be re­verse-engineered, and peo­ple talk­ing to friends.

“So the total gain to so­ci­ety may be 100, but only 40 is cap­tured by me,” Shah said. Each firm there­fore un­der­in­vests in re­search, and that mar­ket fail­ure is the case for the state. {059-C01}

Varma was not con­vinced. The state runs on co­erced taxes, he ar­gued, so its every act car­ries a moral cost, and pos­i­tive ex­ter­nal­i­ties can be found al­most ev­ery­where. Pointing to one is not enough. {059-C02}
## The case for con­tract­ing

On what to fund, they agreed. India should free-ride grate­fully on knowl­edge made abroad, Shah said, and spend pub­lic money only on prob­lems no­body else will solve, such as COVID in hot, humid Indian homes. {059-C06}

Then came the heart of the paper. Like a com­pany choos­ing be­tween its own can­teen and a caterer, the state can “make” re­search in ver­ti­cal or­gan­i­sa­tions such as ISRO, DRDO and CSIR, or “buy” it from uni­ver­si­ties and firms. {#canteen}

Making de­feats the pur­pose, Shah ar­gued, be­cause the spillovers stay sealed in­side the state. “Our ob­jec­tive is not to make the Indian state great, our ob­jec­tive is to make India great.” {059-C08}

Buying also suits re­search, which needs rival path­ways and the free­dom to fail. Inside gov­ern­ment, Shah said, ap­provals lock onto one path and au­di­tors treat fail­ure as wrong­do­ing. {059-C09}
Varma was won over on the how. Spreading re­search across uni­ver­si­ties and firms, he said, pro­duces ex­actly what the title of a Matt Ridley talk de­scribes: *When Ideas Have Sex*. {059-J19}
## Doubts and a blue­print

His wor­ries were about India. American ex­am­ples rest on in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture, such as the rule of law, Varma said, while Indian schol­ars wait years for grant money: “our in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture is in­vis­i­ble be­cause it is non-existent.” {059-J04}
Why would of­fi­cials give up bud­gets and sub­or­di­nates? Change must come from the top, Shah said, bor­row­ing from Vijay Kelkar: “the politi­cians are the en­trepreneurs”. {059-C11}

The paper sketches a 20-year path: new chap­ters in the General Financial Rules al­low­ing grants and cost-plus con­tracts, found­ing doc­u­ments that re­quire con­tract­ing out, and teams that mix sci­ence, en­gi­neer­ing and law. {059-C12}

Reform one or two of the five big sci­ence or­gan­i­sa­tions that mat­ter, Shah said, and start one or two new ones, among them an Indian NIH and a DARPA-like agency. “So we’re not propos­ing an up­heaval, we’re propos­ing a 20 year jour­ney.”
## Long games

Varma held his ground on the why, rec­om­mend­ing Matt Ridley’s *How Innovation Works*, a bot­tom-up ac­count of in­no­va­tion whose au­thor, he thought, would agree with much of his scep­ti­cism. {059-R02}

Shah’s own pick was Huntsville, Alabama, a cow town seeded with German rocket sci­en­tists. It echoed, he said, an old Gandhian idea: peo­ple who each dug into a sin­gle vil­lage after in­de­pen­dence. A few re­mark­able peo­ple in one place, he said, are “dis­pro­por­tion­ately pow­er­ful once you’re will­ing to play for the long term”. {059-S09}

second.label: Knowledge spillovers
second.head: Mum’s not the word
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why Israel’s engineers talk and Apple’s stay silent

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Israel’s blabbermouth engineers

body: Nobody out­side Apple knows what it will an­nounce next. In Silicon Valley, Ajay Shah said, non-disclosure agree­ments and a com­mer­cial cul­ture keep employees’ mouths shut: a low-spillover en­vi­ron­ment. {059-S02}[[x2]]

Israel is the op­po­site. “It is said of the glo­ri­ous Israeli in­no­va­tion ecosys­tem that the sci­en­tists and the en­gi­neers are blab­ber mouths,” he said. Nearly all of them went through con­scrip­tion, often with real fight­ing, and the friend­ships formed there cut across com­pany lines.

Every firm’s knowl­edge leaks qui­etly to oth­ers through net­works of army bud­dies, Shah said, and the same hap­pens in India. That is why firms cap­ture only part of what their re­search is worth, and why they spend too lit­tle on it. {059-C01}

quote.text: If you don’t lock up peo­ple in a vault in the desert, then there will be knowl­edge spillovers.

third.head: From Tata to the state

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Tata origins of TIFR and BARC

body: Two of the proud­est names in Indian sci­ence, TIFR and BARC, began as pri­vate projects of the Tata group[[x4]], Ajay Shah re­minded lis­ten­ers. After in­de­pen­dence they were handed to the Union gov­ern­ment, which paid for ev­ery­thing and made their staff civil ser­vants. {059-S01}

That “make” tem­plate was re­peated[[x3]] across the ICMR, ICAR, DRDO, CSIR and ISRO: ver­ti­cal gov­ern­ment or­gan­i­sa­tions, often sited away from the main cen­tres of eco­nomic ac­tiv­ity, build­ing things in-house.
They can do re­mark­able things. They sent a craft to orbit Mars, Shah said, at a claimed total cost lower than that of the film *The Martian*. {#martian}
Shah does not sec­ond-guess the choices made after 1947. “Maybe that was the only way avail­able then,” he said. His ques­tion is whether today’s India needs a dif­fer­ent model.

p2.title: Make or buy
p2.deck: How the state should fund science: Ajay Shah’s paper, and Amit Varma’s doubts about it

from1.head: Hire the lab, don’t build it

quote.text: So each in­di­vid­ual, each firm tends to un­der­in­vest in in­no­va­tive ac­tiv­i­ties, and that’s the mar­ket fail­ure.

box.title: The blueprint on the table
box.text: *Rethinking innovation policy in India: Amplifying spillovers through contracting-out*, by RA Mashelkar, Ajay Shah and Susan Thomas, ar­gues that the state should buy re­search rather than make it. Amit Varma, who doubts its why, rec­om­mended it him­self. {059-J06}

sections.label: The why
sections.head: Ideas leak, so firms skimp
sections.caption: why ideas leak
body: Left to it­self, Ajay Shah said, a free so­ci­ety will set about build­ing knowl­edge and in­no­vat­ing. “People will do it.” The ques­tion, as al­ways, is whether there is a mar­ket fail­ure. {#default}

There is, he said, and it is the same one that af­fects higher ed­u­ca­tion: knowl­edge spillovers. Publications get read, patents spell out in­ven­tions in full, and ma­chines can be re­verse-engineered and copied.
A lab of total se­crecy is pos­si­ble in the­ory, Shah said, but in re­al­ity knowl­edge al­ways spills over. People talk. “That’s called com­mu­nity.”
If so­ci­ety gains 100 from an in­no­va­tion and the in­no­va­tor keeps only 40, he said, every firm will un­der­in­vest. {059-C01}
## Closing the gap

The rem­edy is for the state to raise taxes and spend them in ways that cre­ate high spillovers, so that knowl­edge dif­fuses through so­ci­ety. Shah’s rough num­bers for India: if 100 is the right level of spend­ing and firms are at 60, the gov­ern­ment could fill the gap of 40. {#sixty}
Such ques­tions, he said, de­serve first prin­ci­ples rather than a de­fault of “Oh, yeah, sci­ence is very good” and more money for gov­ern­ment labs.
~ The money comes at a price. The gov­ern­ment, Shah said, “uses vi­o­lence, it uses co­er­cion” to ex­tract taxes. That was where Amit Varma’s ob­jec­tions would begin.

quote.text: So each in­di­vid­ual, each firm tends to un­der­in­vest in in­no­va­tive ac­tiv­i­ties, and that’s the mar­ket fail­ure.

sections.label: The first doubt
sections.head: Seen, unseen and taxed
sections.caption: the cost of state action
body: Amit Varma’s first ob­jec­tion went to the root. “Every act of gov­ern­ment is an act of vi­o­lence,” he said, the head­line of a col­umn he once wrote: the state ex­ists on taxes raised by co­er­cion. {059-R08}

Political philoso­phies, he ar­gued, dif­fer mainly on when that vi­o­lence is jus­ti­fied. {059-C02} Positive ex­ter­nal­i­ties can be found in al­most any­thing, so in­no­va­tion ranks below rule of law, de­fence and basic in­fra­struc­ture.

Ajay Shah was “very sym­pa­thetic”. Every rupee the gov­ern­ment raises, he and Vijay Kelkar have ar­gued, costs about three ru­pees of GDP[[x9]], through col­lec­tion, com­pli­ance and the way peo­ple change their be­hav­iour to avoid tax. {059-C04}
## Who pays, who gains

Varma took the test as nec­es­sary but not suf­fi­cient. He cited Suyash Rai’s ar­gu­ment against de­mon­eti­sa­tion: when one set of peo­ple bears the costs and an­other gets the ben­e­fits, it is im­moral to point to society’s over­all gain.
Shah ar­gued that Nehru-era sci­ence and higher ed­u­ca­tion seeded India’s IT in­dus­try. Varma, bor­row­ing Frédéric Bastiat’s phrase[[x10]], called that the seen. {059-J10}

~ The un­seen, he said, was what the money would have done had it stayed with the poor it was taken from, and a top-down mind­set that kept hun­dreds of mil­lions in poverty for decades longer than nec­es­sary. {059-C05}

quote.text: Everybody pays taxes. Even the beg­gar at the traf­fic sig­nal has to buy salt, and there is a tax on that.

portraits.caption: Frédéric Bastiat
portraits.credit: Émile Desmaisons. Lithograph by Auguste-Hilaire Léveillé., public domain

sections.label: The what
sections.head: Free-ride, and say thank you
sections.caption: what India should leave to the world
body: A poor coun­try need not in­vent semi­con­duc­tors, Amit Varma said; it can free-ride on in­no­va­tion else­where. Ajay Shah agreed, with grat­i­tude. “It is the grace of the world that cre­ates all this knowl­edge, and we are the ben­e­fi­cia­ries.” {059-C06}

The tran­sis­tor, Unix and ther­mo­dy­nam­ics were not in­vented in India, Shah said. Cheap solar pan­els exist thanks to Chinese fac­to­ries and re­search in Europe, America and Japan, and Covishield, from Oxford and AstraZeneca, was paid for abroad.
## What only India will do
But some prob­lems no­body abroad will solve. How does COVID spread in Indian heat and hu­mid­ity, in open homes with fans? How do you fly drones at 18,000 feet in Ladakh? {#ladakh}

Vaccines for malaria and chikun­gunya will have to be made here, Shah said, and so will much of the hu­man­i­ties and so­cial sci­ences. He re­called a line he thinks was Heisenberg’s: every elec­tron is the same, and every love is dif­fer­ent. {059-J11}
Varma saw this as the con­verse of sub­sidiar­ity: take ev­ery­thing you can from the world, and build at home only what it won’t give you. {#converse}

~ Told that India’s mos­qui­toes change every two hun­dred kilo­me­tres, Varma ar­gued it was less, and re­called writ­ing a lim­er­ick on the mos­qui­toes of Versova for the *Times of India*. {#limerick}

quote.text: So there is a whole zone in which free rid­ing is good and wise.

sections.label: The how
sections.head: Back more than one horse
sections.caption: make versus buy
body: Every or­gan­i­sa­tion chooses be­tween mak­ing and buy­ing, Ajay Shah said. A com­pany can run its own can­teen or hire a caterer, and then po­lice the con­tract with ran­dom tests for bac­te­ria and gut­ter oil. {#canteen}

Indian sci­ence has been made: civil ser­vants in ISRO, DRDO or CSIR craft­ing “some cool toys in­side the gov­ern­ment”. Buying means con­tract­ing uni­ver­si­ties, pub­lic or pri­vate, and firms. Shah has “ab­so­lutely no con­cern” whether it is Ashoka University or IIT Madras.
There, PhD stu­dents carry knowl­edge out, teach­ing spreads it and firms find civil­ian uses. {059-C08}
## The free­dom to fail

Research is risk, Shah said, and gov­ern­ment hates risk. Approval pro­cesses lock onto one path, in­sid­ers snuff out ri­vals, and au­di­tors can­not ac­cept fail­ure. “How will you ex­plain to the CAG that we failed?” {059-J03}

Contract out, and the state can fund six rival teams for a COVID vac­cine and dou­ble down on the two that work. {#six} Even a tele­scope on the moon, he ar­gued, would get there cheaper and faster by buy­ing.

~ Amit Varma bought the method but not the moon. Landing a craft there, he said, is pro­pa­ganda a poor coun­try should not pay for; erad­i­cat­ing malaria would make the bet­ter ex­am­ple. {#malaria}

quote.text: Research is risk tak­ing, it is raw risk tak­ing, it is peer­ing into the fu­ture and not know­ing what will hap­pen.

sections.label: The way forward
sections.head: Plant the sapling now
sections.caption: the 20-year blueprint
body: Amit Varma’s re­main­ing doubts were about India. NASA, he said, cit­ing the paper, sees some five fraud cases in twenty-five thou­sand con­tracts. {#fraud} In India, con­tract­ing out could be­come a gravy train for cronies.

Ajay Shah agreed these prob­lems can­not be solved quickly. Space ex­cel­lence, he ar­gued, is re­ally con­tract­ing ex­cel­lence: the American equiv­a­lents of India’s General Financial Rules made NASA pos­si­ble. {059-C10}
Officials will not give up their bud­gets will­ingly, he said, but lead­ers can push change, as the Vajpayee pe­riod showed with the National Highways Authority of India.
## Three pil­lars

The paper of­fers “draft­ing in­struc­tions”: new chap­ters in the rules for grants and cost-plus con­tracts, found­ing doc­u­ments that make con­tract­ing out the job, and man­u­als and teams that mix sci­ence, en­gi­neer­ing and law. {059-C12}
India has tried be­fore. NMITLI, at CSIR, gave pri­vate firms money and CSIR’s knowl­edge to turn in­no­va­tions into prod­ucts, and ran suc­cess­fully for some years. {#nmitli} It is no more.
~ Nobody ex­pects this overnight, Shah said. He quoted Larry Summers: if a tree will take 20 years to grow, run out­side and plant the sapling right now. {#summers}

quote.text: To be­come a great suc­cess­ful coun­try in space re­search, what you need is amaz­ing lev­els of ca­pa­bil­ity on how to do gov­ern­ment con­tract­ing.

Whereas if uni­ver­si­ties and pri­vate firms know about nan­otech­nol­ogy, then that knowl­edge spills over and it be­comes ma­te­rial for the en­tire coun­try, for the en­tire econ­omy, and we as a peo­ple be­come bet­ter off.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Rockets, fighters, highways and a cow town: how the state gets science done

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the contracting machine behind NASA
stories.head: The space agency that buys
body: NASA dates, Ajay Shah thinks, from 1958. From its found­ing para­graphs, he said, it was warned against hir­ing its own peo­ple and build­ing things, and told to con­tract out in­stead. {#nasa1958}

It still de­fends its bud­get that way. Give NASA 100 ru­pees, it tells law­mak­ers, and 80 go out to uni­ver­si­ties and pri­vate firms. “Only 20% of the money that goes to NASA stays in­side NASA, 80% goes out as con­tracts,” Shah said. {059-S03}

The con­tract­ing comes in stages, by tech­nol­ogy readi­ness level. Rival uni­ver­si­ties and firms first write early con­cepts; then come de­sign doc­u­ments, then work­ing demos tested in NASA’s of­fice, and fi­nally pro­duc­tion or­ders, such as five of a par­tic­u­lar en­gine.

When in­te­grated cir­cuits ar­rived[[x11]], NASA was ef­fec­tively their only buyer, be­cause space­craft needed minia­tur­i­sa­tion while cir­cuit boards on Earth could stay bulky. All the early chip firms ran on NASA con­tracts. “When the IC came along, it was NASA that smelled blood,” Shah said. {059-S04}

Then there is the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, the con­trol room for NASA’s in­ter­plan­e­tary mis­sions to Mars and Jupiter. It is not a gov­ern­ment fa­cil­ity. It is a long-term con­tract, housed since the 60s at Caltech, a pri­vate uni­ver­sity. {059-S05}

Most peo­ple in India, Shah said, would be shocked to learn this. Caltech, he said, is one of the world’s great en­gi­neer­ing uni­ver­si­ties. Thousands of JPL staff sit be­side its re­searchers, and cof­fee-table con­ver­sa­tions help both.
~ “What hap­pens in NASA doesn’t stay in NASA,” Amit Varma said. {059-J08}
stories.why: NASA’s great­ness, in Shah’s ac­count, is largely a con­tract­ing ma­chine. Sending most of its money out builds ca­pa­bil­ity across the coun­try, has seeded an in­dus­try and makes the bud­get eas­ier to de­fend. {059-C10}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on how NASA contracts out

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s oddball recommendation: a town in Alabama
stories.head: Rocket men in cow country
body: Asked for a rec­om­men­da­tion, Ajay Shah of­fered a place: Huntsville, Alabama. After the Second World War, he said, the Americans and the Soviets raced across oc­cu­pied Europe for the German sci­en­tists be­hind the V-1 and V-2 mis­siles.

Many were diehard Nazis who could not be trusted loose in so­ci­ety. So the American mil­i­tary dumped them in an ob­scure cor­ner of America, kept them in semi-imprisonment for a time and built them a lab. This was “make not buy”, Shah noted.

The sci­en­tists put down roots and raised fam­i­lies. Their chil­dren landed up in school, com­peted with the lo­cals and drove up stan­dards, and over a cou­ple of gen­er­a­tions the hick town be­came one of the world’s great R&D cap­i­tals. {059-S08}
~ Amit Varma hoped the story was not lead­ing to a nor­ma­tive place: “Let’s find 200 Nazis and round them up.” {059-J05}
stories.why: Talent com­pounds when planted in one place, Shah ar­gued: seed a town with a few re­mark­able peo­ple and give it gen­er­a­tions. Gandhians who each dug into a sin­gle vil­lage showed the same thing. {059-S09}

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah takes the case outside the English-speaking world
stories.head: Private jets, French style
body: Every mil­i­tary, Ajay Shah said, must do some re­search of its own to adapt its equip­ment. Can you put mod­ern night vi­sion on an old T72? {#t72} In India that work is done the “make” way, through DRDO.

France does it dif­fer­ently. The bulk of its mil­i­tary re­search and pro­duc­tion is done by cor­po­ra­tions. The mil­i­tary sets the chal­lenge, “I want ABCD ca­pa­bil­i­ties”, and pri­vate firms do the re­search under gov­ern­ment con­tracts.
Rafale is a great French fighter, Shah said. “It is built in the pri­vate sec­tor. It is de­signed in the pri­vate sec­tor.” {059-S06}
~ The French use a cost-plus con­tract, he said, which is not a grant but ef­fec­tively pays for the pri­vate firm’s risk-taking.
stories.why: Even de­fence can be bought rather than made, in Shah’s ac­count, if the law can share risk. India’s General Financial Rules, he said, have no con­cept of grants or cost-plus con­tracts. {#gfr}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on French military R&D

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s answer to officials who won’t let go
stories.head: The road less built
body: Why would of­fi­cials who con­trol bud­gets and staff ever give work away? Amit Varma asked. Change, Ajay Shah said, comes from politi­cians, not of­fi­cials. {059-C11}

India’s high­ways used to be built by the Public Works Department. In the Vajpayee pe­riod, Shah said, the lead­er­ship de­cided the gov­ern­ment should give out con­tracts to pri­vate builders in­stead, and the National Highways Authority of India was built for it. {059-S07}
From the ground up, NHAI was a “buy” or­gan­i­sa­tion. “It doesn’t have the en­gi­neers who will go make a road,” Shah said. Its en­gi­neers and lawyers write con­tracts in­stead.
~ It is far from fin­ished, he said: NHAI has still not learned how to do PPP high­ways prop­erly. But the shift hap­pened, be­cause at the lead­er­ship level “peo­ple got the point”.
stories.why: Structural re­form of the Indian state is pos­si­ble once lead­ers grasp the idea, Shah ar­gued. It takes gen­er­a­tions, but India al­ready has a work­ing prece­dent for ex­actly this kind of tran­si­tion.

quiz.q: Why, according to Ajay Shah, are Israel’s scientists and engineers said to be blabbermouths?
quiz.a: Conscription: army friend­ships cut across firms, so knowl­edge leaks through net­works of bud­dies.

quiz.q: Which private university houses NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, the control room for interplanetary missions?
quiz.a: Caltech, under a long-term NASA con­tract that has run since the 60s.

quiz.q: Which Indian organisation does Ajay Shah offer as proof that the state can switch from make to buy?
quiz.a: The National Highways Authority of India, set up in the Vajpayee pe­riod.

quiz.q: Which French fighter, according to Ajay Shah, was designed and built in the private sector?
quiz.a: The Rafale, de­vel­oped by pri­vate firms under gov­ern­ment re­search con­tracts.

glossary.def: Knowledge or ben­e­fit that leaks from its maker to oth­ers
Doing work in-house, or con­tract­ing it out and polic­ing the con­tract
Doing each job at the most local level of gov­ern­ment pos­si­ble
Technology readi­ness level, from early con­cept to near-finished prod­uct
Not a grant, but a con­tract that pays for risk-taking
General Financial Rules, writ­ten for risk-free gov­ern­ment pur­chases

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 59. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Werner Heisenberg (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 de); Raghunath Anant Mashelkar (Fir0002, GFDL 1.2); Frédéric Bastiat (Émile Desmaisons. Lithograph by Auguste-Hilaire Léveillé., public domain); Matt Ridley (Chris McAndrew, CC BY 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon, Apple and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: Rethinking innovation policy in India: Amplifying spillovers through contracting-out
shelf.creator: RA Mashelkar, Ajay Shah and Susan Thomas
shelf.why: A clear, rig­or­ous paper ar­gu­ing that the state should ‘buy’ rather than ‘make’ in­no­va­tion by con­tract­ing R&D out, with a con­crete 20-year blue­print.

shelf.title: How Innovation Works: And Why It Flourishes in Freedom
shelf.creator: Matt Ridley
shelf.why: Ridley shows in­no­va­tion as a bot­tom-up process emerg­ing from within so­ci­ety.

shelf.title: Huntsville, Alabama
shelf.why: A cow town seeded with re­lo­cated German rocket sci­en­tists be­came a world R&D cap­i­tal over gen­er­a­tions.

shelf.title: Why Talent Comes in Clusters (Episode 8)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why the bright­est peo­ple con­cen­trate in places like Silicon Valley and Bell Labs, and how a clus­ter be­comes a mag­net for more tal­ent, helped by friendly reg­u­la­tion and a cul­ture where it is okay to fail.

shelf.title: Science Policy Resolution of 1958
shelf.why: Ajay calls it ‘stirring’ and ‘goose­bumps material’: a dream of build­ing India on ra­tio­nal­ism, be­yond su­per­sti­tion, with sci­ence as a way of life.

shelf.title: When Ideas Have Sex
shelf.creator: Matt Ridley
shelf.why: Ridley’s talk on why ideas must col­lide and re­com­bine freely for the best ones to emerge and for so­ci­ety to progress; the hosts apply it to con­tract­ing re­search out to uni­ver­si­ties and firms.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: Every Act of Government Is an Act of Violence
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s core claim that the state runs on co­er­cion, start­ing with taxes, so every state ac­tion car­ries a moral cost that has to be jus­ti­fied; it is why he ranks spend­ing on in­no­va­tion below the rule of law and basic in­fra­struc­ture.

shelf.title: Understanding the State (Episode 25)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The foun­da­tion of the show’s think­ing on gov­ern­ment: the state is a mo­nop­oly on vi­o­lence that acts through co­er­cion, so every in­ter­ven­tion, paid for by taxes, must be jus­ti­fied.

shelf.title: When Should the State Act? (Episode 26)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on mar­ket fail­ure in its pre­cise tech­ni­cal sense (pub­lic goods, ex­ter­nal­i­ties and the rest) and on the nar­row con­di­tions under which the state may in­ter­vene, con­di­tions that are nec­es­sary but not suf­fi­cient.

shelf.title: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Despite the title, an eco­nomic his­tory of India told through the lens of free­dom: the boom after 1869, Nehru’s Fabian so­cial­ism, the lost years from the 1962 war to the Emergency, and the open­ing-up that lifted mil­lions out of poverty.

shelf.title: The Life and Times of the Indian Economy (Episode 387 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Rajeswari Sengupta
shelf.why: A nearly ten-hour tour with Rajeswari Sengupta of India’s growth episodes and fail­ures and the costs of its post-independence eco­nomic choices.

shelf.title: Biju Rao Won’t Bow to Conventional Wisdom (Episode 392 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Biju Rao
shelf.why: One of Amit’s favourite episodes: Biju Rao ar­gues that you can’t make pol­icy from data on a desk in Washington but have to get your hands dirty on the ground, and that India has its own deep tra­di­tion of vil­lage-level de­lib­er­a­tive democ­racy.

shelf.title: India Needs Decentralization (Episode 47)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case for sub­sidiar­ity in a coun­try as large and var­ied as India: do as lit­tle as pos­si­ble at the Union level and push power down to cities, where peo­ple can see and talk to the of­fi­cials re­spon­si­ble for their side­walks.

shelf.title: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why academia has drifted away from real-world prob­lems: jour­nal-based pro­mo­tion and de­part­men­tal in­cen­tives nar­row every dis­ci­pline, fil­ter out cre­ative mav­er­icks and leave aca­demics writ­ing for each other.

shelf.title: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone? (Episode 55)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A first-principles chal­lenge to India’s op­ti­mism about every new road and air­port: in­fra­struc­ture has di­min­ish­ing re­turns, and big re­cent gains brought no com­pa­ra­ble rise in FDI, man­u­fac­tur­ing ex­ports or jobs.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Education (Episode 56)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Decades of both hosts’ think­ing on ed­u­ca­tion packed into about an hour, an episode Amit is proud of.

shelf.title: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Episode 56)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A cri­tique of ‘dig­i­tal pub­lic infrastructure’ such as Aadhaar and UPI: state-backed mo­nop­o­lies cre­ated by co­er­cive power, with­out checks and bal­ances, that crowd out com­pet­ing pri­vate sys­tems.

shelf.title: The industry structure of India’s large firms: IT is the biggest industry
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It sup­ports his one-line sum­mary of the Indian econ­omy (IT and IT-enabled ser­vices sold to the West) and his ar­gu­ment that early sci­ence and higher-education in­vest­ments seeded it.

shelf.title: Covid-19 in the tropics: How will high heat and humidity shape the outcomes?
shelf.creator: Suja Thomas
shelf.why: It il­lus­trates a uniquely Indian ques­tion: how COVID spreads in hot, humid con­di­tions in open, fan-ventilated homes.

shelf.title: Mosquitoes As Big As A Bus
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A light com­pan­ion to the episode’s point that Indian prob­lems, mos­qui­toes in­cluded, are in­tensely local.

shelf.title: The Martian
shelf.creator: Ridley Scott
shelf.why: It is a vivid yard­stick for what a state ‘make’ or­gan­i­sa­tion can achieve.

shelf.title: Why Does It Always Rain On Me?
shelf.creator: Travis
shelf.why: He loves the line ‘Is it be­cause I lied when I was sev­en­teen?’

shelf.title: Only Happy When It Rains
shelf.creator: Garbage
shelf.why: A fit­ting rain song for the mo­ment.

shelf.title: Public Finance at XKDR
shelf.why: XKDR Forum’s re­search pro­gramme on pub­lic fi­nance and gov­ern­ment con­tract­ing, stud­ied field by field to draw gen­eral lessons.

laughs.text: The opener. Amit: ‘I am an or­ganic human being... Organic mat­ter, it’s a great weak­ness, I know, but that’s who I am.’ Ajay, by con­trast, is a ‘bionic man’ with a metal rod in his bone since a crash at nine­teen and a new ti­ta­nium jaw im­plant. Ajay: ‘Sadly, no bat­ter­ies and no CPUs.’ The metal sets air­port se­cu­rity scream­ing, so he prefers half-sleeve shirts when fly­ing.

Ajay on space mis­sions as pro­pa­ganda: ‘there are cheaper ways of doing pro­pa­ganda. You could just fund a cricket team or some­thing... or you know hire a vis­ual ef­fects team and claim that you sent a craft to the moon.’

Ajay on risk-taking under audit: ‘How will you ex­plain to the CAG, we tried this and it did not work? ... You paid salaries, you pur­chased so many parts... and in the end noth­ing worked. Okay, how can it be? We should have a CBI in­ves­ti­ga­tion.’ He blames the ‘Stalinist idea in government’ that ev­ery­thing al­ways works cor­rectly.
Amit on re­search schol­ars wait­ing years for grant money: ‘our in­vis­i­ble in­fra­struc­ture is in­vis­i­ble be­cause it is non-existent.’

Ajay’s Huntsville moral: 200 Nazis dropped into a ‘tiny hick town filled with cows and peas­ants, in three gen­er­a­tions, it turns into magic.’ Amit replies: ‘I hope it’s not lead­ing to a nor­ma­tive place. Let’s find 200 Nazis and round them up, though it won’t be as dif­fi­cult as it seems in the cur­rent day.’

Rain starts mid-recording and Amit launches a pop quiz: ‘Why does it al­ways rain on me?’ Ajay: ‘I don’t know.’ Amit sup­plies Travis and his favourite line, ‘Is it be­cause I lied when I was sev­en­teen?’, then fol­lows with ‘I’m only happy when it rains’ (Garbage).
The NASA sec­tion ends with a twist on the fa­mil­iar ‘what hap­pens here stays here’ line: ‘What hap­pens in NASA doesn’t stay in NASA.’

Told that Indian mos­qui­toes change every two hun­dred kilo­me­tres, Amit says it’s ac­tu­ally less. He re­calls being a pro­fes­sional lim­er­ick writer for the Times of India with a lim­er­ick on the mos­qui­toes of Versova.

Frédéric Bastiat’s ‘the seen and the unseen’: Amit bor­rows the phrase to argue that the IT boom seeded by Nehru-era sci­ence is the seen ef­fect, while the co­erced money and the top-down mind­set are the un­seen costs.

Heisenberg, as quoted by Ajay: ‘every elec­tron is the same and every love is dif­fer­ent.’ He uses it to ex­plain why physics trav­els across bor­ders but the hu­man­i­ties and so­cial sci­ences must be built at home.
Larry Summers, quoted by Ajay against the ob­jec­tion that re­form takes decades: if a tree will take 20 years to grow, run out­side and plant the sapling right now.

Yashwant Sinha’s line that India lives in many dif­fer­ent cen­turies at once, from me­dieval to twenty-first cen­tury. Ajay uses it to de­fend in­vest­ing in fron­tier sci­ence along­side basic prob­lems.

Suyash Rai’s ar­gu­ment against de­mon­eti­sa­tion: be­cause one group bears the costs and an­other gets the ben­e­fits, it is im­moral to jus­tify a pol­icy by say­ing so­ci­ety over­all ben­e­fits. Amit uses it to rebut pure ag­gre­gate cost-benefit rea­son­ing.

DARPA, ‘just legendary’ for tak­ing risks and build­ing en­tirely new tech­nolo­gies such as TCP/IP and driver­less cars on its con­tracts. It is the model for one of the new or­gan­i­sa­tions the paper pro­poses for India.
The 1958 Science Policy Resolution and IIT Bombay (founded 1957). Ajay notes the dates ‘rhyme’, a sign of a gen­er­a­tion of dream­ers try­ing to build India on ra­tio­nal­ism and sci­ence.
Matt Ridley’s ‘When Ideas Have Sex’, which Amit in­vokes for what hap­pens when re­search is spread across uni­ver­si­ties and firms in­stead of sealed in­side the state.
